name: Sumerian written
what: First written at Uruk; spoken until about 2000-1700 BCE, then a learned language until cuneiform ended.
why: A language isolate: no known relatives.

sources.cite: Roger Woodard (ed.), The Cambridge Encyclopedia of the World's Ancient Languages (2004)
Piotr Michalowski, "Sumerian", in The Cambridge Encyclopedia of the World's Ancient Languages (2004); Jerrold Cooper, "Sumerian and Akkadian in Sumer and Akkad", Orientalia 42 (1973)

name: Egyptian written
what: Hieroglyphs from about 3250 BCE; last hieroglyph 394 CE; Coptic spoken into the 1600s.
why: The longest recorded history of any language, about 4,500 years.

sources.cite: Roger Woodard (ed.), The Cambridge Encyclopedia of the World's Ancient Languages (2004)
Jitse Dijkstra, Philae and the End of Ancient Egyptian Religion (2008)

name: Akkadian written
what: First Semitic language written; the diplomatic language of the Bronze Age.
why: Its last known tablet is an astronomical almanac of 79-80 CE.

sources.cite: Roger Woodard (ed.), The Cambridge Encyclopedia of the World's Ancient Languages (2004)
Abraham Sachs and Hermann Hunger; John Hunger and Teije de Jong, "Almanac W22340a from Uruk: the latest datable cuneiform tablet", Zeitschrift für Assyriologie 103 (2014)

name: Elamite written
what: Language of Susa and Anshan; an administrative language of the Persian empire.
why: An isolate.

sources.cite: Roger Woodard (ed.), The Cambridge Encyclopedia of the World's Ancient Languages (2004)

name: Hittite written
what: Archives of Hattusa; words appear at Kanesh from about 1900 BCE.
why: The oldest written Indo-European language.

sources.cite: Roger Woodard (ed.), The Cambridge Encyclopedia of the World's Ancient Languages (2004)

name: Minoan written
what: Written in Linear A.
why: Unknown language.

sources.cite: Roger Woodard (ed.), The Cambridge Encyclopedia of the World's Ancient Languages (2004)

name: Etruscan written
what: About 13,000 inscriptions; readable but poorly understood.
why: A non-Indo-European language in Italy; Emperor Claudius wrote its history (lost).

sources.cite: Giuliano and Larissa Bonfante, The Etruscan Language: An Introduction (2nd ed., 2002)

name: Latin written
what: From the Lapis Niger; never written out, it turned into the Romance languages.
why: Still the Vatican's official language.

sources.cite: Roger Woodard (ed.), The Cambridge Encyclopedia of the World's Ancient Languages (2004)

name: Old Chinese written
what: Oracle bones of Anyang.

sources.cite: David Keightley, Sources of Shang History: The Oracle-Bone Inscriptions of Bronze Age China (1978)

name: Gothic written
what: Wulfila's Bible.
why: East Germanic, now extinct.

sources.cite: Peter Daniels and William Bright (eds.), The World's Writing Systems (1996)

name: Meroitic written
what: Language of Kush.
why: Poorly understood.

sources.cite: Claude Rilly, La langue du royaume de Méroé (2007)

name: Death of Manx
what: Ned Maddrell, the last native speaker, died 27 December 1974.
why: Revived since; children are again raised speaking it.

sources.cite: George Broderick, Language Death in the Isle of Man (1999)

name: Death of Cornish
what: Dolly Pentreath of Mousehole, often called the last speaker, died in 1777; some speakers lived on later.
why: Revived in the 20th century.

sources.cite: Matthew Spriggs, "Who was the Last Speaker of Cornish?", Cornish Studies 11 (2003)

name: Death of Dalmatian
what: Tuone Udaina of Krk, the last speaker, was killed by a road-mine explosion on 10 June 1898.
why: A Romance language between Italian and Romanian.

sources.cite: Matteo Bartoli, Das Dalmatische (1906)

name: Death of Ubykh
what: Tevfik Esenç died 7 October 1992 in Turkey.
why: Had about 80 consonants; its speakers were expelled from the Caucasus in 1864.

sources.cite: Georges Dumézil, Le verbe oubykh (1975); Hewitt, "Ubykh" (Encyclopedia of Language and Linguistics, 2006)

name: Death of Eyak
what: Marie Smith Jones died 21 January 2008 in Anchorage.
why: An Alaskan relative of Athabaskan.

sources.cite: Michael Krauss, "Native languages of Alaska", in The Vanishing Voices of the Pacific Rim (2007); Alaska Native Language Center obituary of Marie Smith Jones (2008)

name: Death of Livonian
what: Grizelda Kristiņa, the last native speaker, died 2 June 2013.
why: A Finnic language of the Latvian coast.

sources.cite: Tiit-Rein Viitso, "Livonian", in Uralic Languages (2nd ed., 2022); news of Grizelda Kristiņa's death (2013)

name: Death of Old Prussian
what: Died out around 1700 after plague and Germanisation.
why: A Baltic language; the name Prussia comes from it.

sources.cite: William Schmalstieg, Studies in Old Prussian (1976)

name: Death of Crimean Gothic
what: Recorded by Busbecq in the 1560s; gone by the 1700s.
why: The last Germanic language of the east.

sources.cite: MacDonald Stearns, Crimean Gothic: Analysis and Etymology of the Corpus (1978)

name: Death of Yahgan
what: Cristina Calderón died 16 February 2022.
why: Spoken at the southern tip of the Americas.

sources.cite: Reports of the death of Cristina Calderón, last native speaker of Yahgan, Chile (February 2022)

name: Death of Tasmanian languages
what: Fanny Cochrane Smith recorded songs in 1899-1903 and died in 1905.
why: Wiped out by colonial violence and disease; palawa kani is a reconstruction.

sources.cite: Terry Crowley and Robert Dixon, "Tasmanian", in Handbook of Australian Languages 2 (1981)

name: Sumerian (as a spoken language)
what: Stopped being spoken somewhere between 2000 and 1700 BCE, replaced by Akkadian.
why: It stayed a written and sacred language for 1,800 years more.

sources.cite: Piotr Michalowski, "Sumerian", in The Cambridge Encyclopedia of the World's Ancient Languages (2004); Jerrold Cooper, "Sumerian and Akkadian in Sumer and Akkad", Orientalia 42 (1973)

name: Akkadian (last tablet)
what: The latest datable cuneiform tablet, an almanac for 79-80 CE.
why: Ends 3,000 years of cuneiform.

sources.cite: Abraham Sachs and Hermann Hunger; John Hunger and Teije de Jong, "Almanac W22340a from Uruk: the latest datable cuneiform tablet", Zeitschrift für Assyriologie 103 (2014)

name: Egyptian hieroglyphs (last inscription)
what: Last dated hieroglyphic inscription, Philae, 24 August 394.
why: Within a few generations no one could read them until Champollion (1822).

sources.cite: Jitse Dijkstra, Philae and the End of Ancient Egyptian Religion (2008)

name: Turkish switch to the Latin alphabet
what: Atatürk replaced the Arabic script with Latin letters in November 1928.
why: Literacy rose, and Ottoman writing became unreadable to most Turks within a generation.

sources.cite: Geoffrey Lewis, The Turkish Language Reform: A Catastrophic Success (1999)

name: Soviet move to Cyrillic
what: Between 1936 and 1940 the USSR moved its Turkic and other languages from Latin (introduced in the 1920s) to Cyrillic.
why: Two script changes in 15 years; several states switched to Latin again after 1991.

sources.cite: Lenore Grenoble, Language Policy in the Soviet Union (2003)

name: Simplified Chinese characters
what: The PRC issued its first list of simplified characters in 1956.
why: Taiwan, Hong Kong and Macau kept traditional characters.

sources.cite: Ping Chen, Modern Chinese: History and Sociolinguistics (1999)

name: Vietnamese Latin script (Quốc ngữ)
what: Alexandre de Rhodes published a Latin-script Vietnamese dictionary in 1651; French rule made it official in the early 1900s.
why: Replaced Chinese characters and chữ Nôm.

sources.cite: John DeFrancis, Colonialism and Language Policy in Viet Nam (1977)

name: Hangul announced
what: King Sejong published Hunminjeongeum in 1446.
why: Elites kept Chinese characters for centuries; Hangul became standard only in the 20th century.

sources.cite: Ki-Moon Lee and Robert Ramsey, A History of the Korean Language (2011)
